name: Cosplay body paint

card.summary: Water-based or specialty paint applied over skin so a cosplayer's skin tone and markings match a character, giving a costume a full-body match.
card.note: Use paints made for skin; latex and some colorants can cause allergic reactions.

quick.overview:
Cosplay body paint is paint or makeup used to turn a cosplayer's skin into a character's: a blue, green or grey complexion, painted markings, or a different overall tone. It changes how the whole body looks for a costume rather than improving the person's natural appearance, and it washes off afterward.

In Japanese cosplay the practice of matching the skin tone of non-human or fictional characters is called ishoku-hada. Body painting more broadly has a long history, and modern water-based face and body paints are designed to be non-toxic and easy to remove.
quick.how: Cosplayers use water-based face and body paints applied with brushes, sponges or an airbrush, sometimes with temporary tattoos or markers for fine markings. Paint is chosen to match a character reference, often with a setting product, and removed with soap and water at the end of the day.
quick.risks: Reported cautions are about allergy and skin sensitivity: stop using a paint if skin shows signs of reaction, avoid damaged skin, check ingredients, and use only products made for skin. Liquid latex can cause contact allergy and heat build-up with long wear. Some colorants are not approved for use near eyes or on lips.

lead: Cosplay body paint is the use of face and body paint to change skin color and add markings so that a cosplayer matches a character. Cosplay is a performance art in which participants wear costumes to portray specific characters, and its practitioners often modify their bodies with makeup, contact lenses, hair color and temporary tattoos to match.[1]

Skin-tone matching is part of this. In Japan, the practice of using body paint to match the skin tones of non-human or fictional characters has its own term, ishoku-hada.[1] The tradition of painting the body is far older: face painting dates from Paleolithic times, and body painting festivals such as the World Bodypainting Festival, begun in 1998, now draw artists worldwide.[2]
No clinical research was found on cosplay body paint. Safety notes in general body-painting references recommend skin-safe products, patch testing and caution with latex.[2]

angle.goal: Skin tone and body markings for a costume
chain: Paint is applied over skin to match a character
Skin color and markings match the reference
angle.text: Body paint changes the visible color and markings of the skin for the duration of a costume, letting a cosplayer match characters whose skin tone or markings differ from their own.

paras: Cosplayers modify skin tone through makeup and, in Japan, ishoku-hada; they also use temporary tattoos, permanent marker, body paint and, rarely, permanent tattoos to copy a character's marks.[1] Paints are typically applied by hand, brush, sponge or airbrush.[2]

Modern water-based face and body paints are made to strict guidelines, are usually non-toxic and non-allergenic and wash off easily; fluorescent versions glow under ultraviolet light.[2] Liquid latex can cause contact allergy and heat stroke with long wear.[2]

Guidance cited in reference works advises testing for allergy where possible, avoiding damaged or inflamed skin, checking ingredients because some colorants are not approved for the eye area or lips, and never using products not formulated for the body.[2] California's Proposition 65 sets stricter limits on lead in cosmetics.[2]

Cosplay grew from fan costuming in the twentieth century; the word was coined in 1983 by Nobuyuki Takahashi, and events such as the World Cosplay Summit began in Nagoya in 2003.[1] Questions about skin-tone portrayal, including blackface, brownface and yellowface, are debated in the community.[1]

timeline.event: The term cosplay is coined in Japan.[1]
World Cosplay Summit begins in Nagoya.[1]
